judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 137. It bars one more group of inmates from serving time at home on an electronic monitor. The Department of Corrections may let some inmates serve part of a sentence at home, tracked by an ankle monitor. The program is only for crimes the law does not class as violent. The law already lists many inmates who may not take part, such as those convicted of domestic abuse or a sex offense. The act adds one more group. It covers people convicted of causing a crash that badly hurt someone else while driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. The rest of the act only tidies wording. The Oklahoma House passed it 72-18. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to override the Governor's veto of Senate Bill 713. It makes wind farms fit warning lights that stay off until a plane is near. Wind turbines carry red warning lights for aircraft, and these usually blink all night. The act calls for a system that keeps the lights off until it detects a plane nearby, where federal aviation and radio regulators approve one. From January 1, 2026, a new wind farm may not start running until it has applied for such a system. An existing wind farm must apply when it is rebuilt or signs a new long-term deal to sell its power. Once approval comes, the system must be fitted within two years. The wind farm pays for it. A county may issue bonds to help pay for systems on older wind farms. A power company whose rates are set by the state may ask to recover its costs from customers. Wind farms that sit wholly on land their owner holds outright are not covered. The Oklahoma House voted 68-17 to override the veto. The Senate had already done the same, so the bill became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 3644. It sets rules for hospitals to spot and treat dangerous blood clots. The act is named the Blake Burgess Act. It deals with blood clots in a deep vein, usually in the leg or arm, which can travel to the lungs and kill. Every hospital with an emergency room, and every outpatient surgery center, must adopt policies based on best practice. The policies must cover how to judge a patient's risk with a recognized tool, and how to treat a clot once it is found. Clinical staff who do not hold a professional license must be trained on them every year. The State Department of Health must set up a statewide record of clot cases. From July 1, 2027, each hospital with an emergency room must report its cases to it every year. Assisted living centers must check new residents for signs of a clot and give them a leaflet on the warning signs. The Oklahoma House passed it 68-21. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 3834. It lets the state help pay for trials of ibogaine, a psychedelic drug studied as a treatment for addiction. The State Department of Health may contract with a drug developer to run trials aimed at winning federal approval for ibogaine, if money is available. The developer must already have a similar deal with at least one other state. It must match the state's money dollar for dollar and run the trials in Oklahoma, using local clinicians and patients where it can. It must also plan how Oklahomans will get the treatment once it is approved, including people who are uninsured or on low incomes. The state gets a share of any profits from the research, in line with what it paid. That money goes into a fund for research and programs on brain injury, opioid addiction and other mental health conditions. Doctors may not be disciplined just for suggesting that a patient join a trial. The act takes effect on November 1, 2026. The Oklahoma House passed it 69-21. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 4071. It sets up a one-time $250 state deposit into a child's federal Trump Account. A Trump Account is a savings account for children created by federal law. Under the act the State Treasurer may put $250 once into the account of an eligible child. The child must be under eighteen when the application is made, a United States citizen with a Social Security number, and living in Oklahoma. Payments go out in the order applications are checked, and only as money reaches a new state fund set up for the purpose. The act creates that fund but does not itself put money into it. No payment may break a federal limit. The Oklahoma House passed it 61-30. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 1727. It opens the state's free tuition scholarship to more teachers' children and gives students longer to sign up. Oklahoma's Promise pays college tuition for students from families under an income limit who sign up while in school and keep its rules. The act adds the children of classroom teachers with at least ten years in Oklahoma public schools. For them the family income limit is 700 percent of the federal poverty level, far above the usual limit. Principals, superintendents and other administrators do not count as teachers for this purpose. Other students keep the usual limits, set by family size: $60,000 with up to two children, $70,000 with three or four, and $80,000 with five or more. Students may now sign up as late as December 31 of their last year of high school. Nobody aged 21 or older may join. The Oklahoma House passed it 60-27. The Governor signed it.
